q: can I give Motrin to my 8 month old for fever
text: Yes, ibuprofen (Motrin) can be given to an 8-month-old for fever: acetaminophen (Tylenol) and ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) help reduce fever in children, according to MedlinePlus [6]. Do not use ibuprofen in children younger than 6 months, and know your child's weight before giving it [6]. Give it every 6 to 8 hours [6]. The NHS says you can give either acetaminophen or ibuprofen if your child is distressed or uncomfortable, checking the packaging or leaflet to make sure the medicine is suitable, or speaking to a pharmacist or doctor if you are not sure [3]. Do not give ibuprofen to a child who has chickenpox, is dehydrated, or has asthma unless a doctor recommends it [2]. Keep giving plenty of fluids, and if your baby is breastfed, continue to breastfeed as normal [3]. Get medical advice if you are worried or if the medicine is not helping [3].

q: my son threw up twice this morning, what should I give him to drink
text: For vomiting, the priority is to keep giving fluids to prevent dehydration, according to the SEUP [3]. Wait 20 minutes after a vomit, then give oral rehydration solution, 2–5 ml every 5 minutes for an hour [3]. Watch how well your son takes it: if he keeps the fluids down, you can slowly increase how often you offer them [3]. Do not use homemade solutions or commercial soft drinks [3]. q: how do I know if my child is getting dehydrated from vomiting
text:
Dehydration happens when the body loses more fluid than it takes in, and vomiting is one of the causes [1]. The main risk of vomiting is dehydration, according to the SEUP [3].

To prevent it, give oral rehydration fluids — the kind you get over the counter [2]. When your child vomits, wait 20 minutes, then give oral rehydration solution, 2–5 ml every 5 minutes for an hour [5]. If they keep it down, you can slowly increase how often you give it [5]. Don't use homemade solutions or fizzy drinks [5]. Sports drinks can help with mild dehydration but may not replace important nutrients and minerals [2].

If your child is floppy, vomits a lot, or won't take fluids, see your paediatrician [3]. If you think they are severely dehydrated, call your doctor — severe dehydration may need fluids through a vein in hospital [2].

q: my 5 year old has been coughing all night, what can I do
text:
A cough that keeps a child awake at night is common in preschool children, and viral respiratory infections are the main cause of this kind of coughing at this age, according to the SEUP [2]. Asthma can also cause a cough that is worse at night, along with a feeling of breathlessness [5].

There is no home remedy for the cough itself in these pages. What they describe is how to recognise a breathing problem: watch for the chest and ribs pulling in when they breathe, breathing faster than normal, or a whistling sound as air comes out [5]. A blue tinge around the lips means the oxygen in the blood is low [5].

If your child has a severe feeling of breathlessness, continuous coughing or trouble speaking, that is a serious sign [5].

q: my son has been coughing for a week after a cold
text:
A cough that lingers after a cold is common, and cold symptoms can last 10 to 14 days, according to MedlinePlus [6]. If the cough comes in bouts that are worse at night, or your son makes a "whoop" sound gasping between coughs, that can be whooping cough, according to the NHS [4]. Whooping cough starts like a cold and the cough can last several weeks or months [4].

There is no specific treatment for a cold; keep him comfortable and offer fluids. If you think it may be whooping cough, ask your doctor, who may give medicine to shorten the illness [3]. See your doctor if he is getting worse or not getting better [3].

q: he has a cough but no fever and is eating normally
text:
A cough without fever, with normal eating, is usually a common cold or similar mild infection — a high temperature is the body's natural response to fighting infections like coughs and colds, according to the NHS [1].

Keep offering fluids and let him rest; there is no need to treat a fever he does not have. If a fever does appear, the NHS says not to undress or sponge him down to cool him, not to cover him in too many clothes or bedclothes, and not to give aspirin to a child under 16 [1]. Paracetamol or ibuprofen are the usual medicines for fever and discomfort, with paracetamol the first choice, according to PUC Chile [4]; the dose depends on his weight.

Get urgent help if he is under 3 months and has a temperature of 38C (100.4 °F) or higher, is 3 to 6 months and has 39C (102.2 °F) or higher, has a rash with the fever, stops wanting to eat or is not his usual self, or shows signs of dehydration such as nappies that are not very wet, sunken eyes, and no tears when crying [1].

q: my daughter has red spots all over her stomach and they appeared today
text:
Red spots that appear suddenly and itch a lot are often hives, which in childhood are usually caused by an infection rather than an allergy, according to the SEUP [3]. The spots are raised, red patches that move around — fading in one area as they appear in another — and may come with swelling of the hands, feet, elbows or face [3].

Hives can usually be treated at home, according to the NHS [5]. If there is swelling around your child's mouth or they are struggling to breathe, that is an emergency [5].

Keep an eye out for other symptoms too: measles causes a red, blotchy rash that usually starts on the head and spreads down the body, along with fever, cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis and small white spots inside the mouth, according to MedlinePlus [2].

q: my 2 year old has little red bumps on his legs and keeps scratching them
text:
It is common for a young child to get an itchy rash, and hives is one cause, according to the NHS [1]. Hives look like raised, itchy bumps or patches that vary in size and can be close together in groups [1].

A pharmacist can give you advice about antihistamine treatment to help a hives rash, though this treatment might not be suitable for young children [7]. Tell the pharmacist if your child has a long-term condition, because they might not be able to take antihistamines [7].

Get help immediately if your child's lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly become swollen, if they are breathing very fast or struggling to breathe, if their throat feels tight or they are struggling to swallow, if their skin, tongue or lips turn blue, grey or pale, if they suddenly become very confused, drowsy or dizzy, if they faint and cannot be woken up, or if they are limp, floppy or not responding like they normally do [7].

q: these spots dont seem to bother her but there are more every morning
text:
Spots that don't bother your child and keep appearing each morning are described by the NHS as part of nappy rash, which is common in babies and can usually be treated at home [2]. Nappy rash can look like red or raw patches on the bottom or the whole nappy area, or spots, pimples or blisters that may be red or brown [2]. It can also come with scaly, dry skin, an itchy or painful bottom, or your baby seeming uncomfortable or distressed [2].

Keep the nappy area clean and dry, change nappies often, and use a barrier cream at each change; ask a pharmacist for advice if it is not settling [2].

See your doctor if the rash spreads, blisters, or your baby seems unwell or in pain [2].
sources: [2] NHS — "Nappy rash" (2026), section "Nappy rash", p. 1 — https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring

q: my 6 year old fell from the bed and hit the back of his head
text:
Most head injuries are not serious, but it is important to get medical help for any symptoms, according to the NHS [2]. A head injury is a blow to the head, usually from a fall, and the usual symptoms are headache, confusion, brief memory loss, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and drowsiness [1].

For a 6-year-old who fell from a bed, the SEUP says to watch for these signs over the first 24 hours: intense or worsening headache that does not improve with paracetamol or ibuprofen, repeated vomiting, confusion or disorientation, behaviour changes, trouble speaking or walking, and blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears [4]. If there is headache, you can give ibuprofen or paracetamol in the dose your doctor indicates [6]. Rest from physical activity and screens for 24 to 48 hours, then return gradually [4]. They can eat normally and sleep, though after a more significant knock it is worth waking them every 4 hours [6].

Go to the emergency department if any of those symptoms appear, or if the fall was from more than one metre [5].

q: he fell off the couch and vomited once about an hour later

text:
A knock on the head is a head injury, and vomiting is one of the symptoms it can cause, according to the SEUP [7]. Vomiting once after a fall is a reason to be seen in the emergency department, and so is a fall from more than a metre or a child under three months [1].

While you travel, keep the child with you and do not leave them alone. If they are sleepy, floppy, very thirsty, have sunken eyes, cry without tears or pass little urine, that needs urgent attention [3]. Vomiting that is green, contains blood or looks like coffee grounds also needs urgent attention [3].

q: what foods should I start with for a baby who just turned 6 months
text: At around 6 months, milk alone no longer meets all your baby's energy and nutrient needs, so solid foods are needed alongside it, according to the WHO [1]. Start with small amounts and increase them gradually as your baby grows, and build up the variety and texture of foods over time [1]. Give 2–3 meals a day at 6 to 8 months, and keep breastfeeding on demand alongside [1]. At the beginning, how much your baby eats matters less than getting used to eating — most energy and nutrients still come from breast milk or first infant formula [2]. Introduce one food at a time so you can spot any allergic reaction, such as a rash, diarrhoea or vomiting, according to MedlinePlus [5]. Do not give honey before age 1, and avoid cow's milk and unpasteurised foods before age 1 [5].

q: how much water can a 9 month old drink
text: For a 9-month-old, breast milk or formula stays the main drink, and water comes mainly from food and milk rather than large amounts on its own. The WHO says to keep breastfeeding frequently, on demand, up to 2 years or beyond, and to feed 3–4 meals a day for babies 9 to 23 months, with 1–2 snacks if needed [1]. The AEP says that between 6 and 12 months breast milk remains the main food, so keep feeding on demand without reducing the number of feeds; if a baby over 6 months has at least 4–5 breastfeeds a day, no other milk source is needed [2]. During illness, the WHO says to increase fluid intake, including how often you breastfeed, and to offer soft, favourite foods [1]. Do not add salt to a baby's food: babies need very little, and their kidneys are too immature to handle much salt [2].

q: my baby refuses vegetables but eats fruit all day
text: A baby who refuses vegetables but eats fruit is a common picky-eating pattern, and the CDC has tips to help picky eaters try new foods [1]. Keep offering a variety of foods, including vegetables with bitter flavours such as broccoli, cauliflower, spinach and cabbage, alongside fruit, so your baby gets used to them over time [2]. Offer three meals a day plus their usual milk feeds, and include iron-rich foods like meat, fish, fortified cereals, beans and lentils [2]. As they become a more confident eater, offer more mashed, lumpy and finger foods, and let them feed themselves [2]. Don't add salt or sugar to their food or cooking water [2].

q: my daughter is 13 months and still mostly drinks formula
text: At 13 months, formula alone is not enough — she needs solid foods alongside it. Around 6 months, a baby's energy and nutrient needs start to exceed what milk alone provides, so complementary foods are needed [2]. Continue milk feeds, but offer 3–4 meals a day plus 1–2 snacks, according to the WHO [2]. Start with small amounts and increase them gradually as she grows, and build up the consistency and variety of foods [2]. Keep practising good hygiene and handling food safely [2]. If she is unwell, offer more fluids and soft, favourite foods [2]. The WHO recommends breastfeeding continue to 2 years or beyond, with adequate, safe complementary foods from 6 months [3].

q: how often should a newborn poop
text: How often a newborn poops varies from baby to baby — the rhythm and consistency of stools differ from one person to another, according to the SEUP [3]. What matters more is whether the stool is hard and whether passing it hurts: constipation is stool that is too hard, with discomfort or incomplete emptying, and it can come with fewer bowel movements [6]. In a baby under 6 months, keep feeding as usual with breast milk or formula [3]. Do not give laxatives or enemas without asking your doctor [3]. See your doctor if there is blood in the stool, bad belly pain, or the baby vomits many times and cannot keep down solids or liquids [3].

q: my 9 month old suddenly wakes up every two hours at night
text: It is common and normal for a 9-month-old to wake at night: night wakings are physiological, and almost 30% of children still wake at night by one year, according to the PUC Chile manual [2]. Babies this age often need to fall back to sleep on their own, and if they always fall asleep in your arms, they will want the same conditions to go back to sleep [2]. Try to let your baby settle back to sleep alone rather than intervening each time, so a sleep habit does not form [2]. Night terrors are different: they are most common between ages 3 and 7, so they are unlikely at 9 months [1]. If your baby seems unwell, has a fever, or is not feeding or growing well, see your doctor.

q: my 4 year old wakes up coughing only when he lies down
text:
A cough that comes mainly at night or early in the morning is one of the symptoms of asthma in children, according to MedlinePlus [3]. The same pattern — cough, sometimes at night — is described by the SEUP, which notes that in preschool children the usual trigger is a viral respiratory infection [4][5].

Asthma is hard to diagnose in a 4-year-old, because the symptoms look like other childhood illnesses and lung function tests are not possible at this age [6]. Doctors use the history, an exam, a chest X-ray, and allergy tests if there is a history of allergy; sometimes they suggest trying asthma medicine for several weeks to see if the symptoms improve [6].

Get medical help right away if your child has severe coughing, serious breathing problems, or turns very pale or blue in the face, lips or fingernails [3].

q: my son has asthma and is using albuterol more than usual
text:
Using albuterol more often than usual can be a sign the asthma is getting worse, so this needs attention. Asthma attacks happen when the airways narrow and symptoms get worse than usual [4].

Give salbutamol with a spacer (and a mask for small children), never directly into the mouth, according to the SEUP [3]. If there is no clear improvement, go to a health centre [6].

Get urgent help if he is very restless or drowsy, turns blue or pale, breathes faster and faster, his ribs or chest pull in, or he needs inhalations every two hours or less [6].

q: my daughter is breathing faster after running but gets better when she rests
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Breathing difficulty: fast breathing, wheezing, ribs pulling in
text: Fast breathing during running that settles with rest is expected, and a child who is well and has no fever can keep up their physical activity, according to the SEUP [3]. While you are on your way to be seen, keep your daughter calm and let her rest; if she has a fever, the SEUP advises waiting 24 hours without fever before returning to school [3]. Watch her general state and her breathing — ribs pulling in, the chest sinking, fast breathing or tiring when walking or running, or chest pain when breathing [3]. Get urgent help if her general state worsens, if she is limp, sleepy or very irritable, or if breathing difficulty appears [3].

q: she is making a strange noise when she breathes but is still smiling
text:
A strange noise when breathing can be croup: an inflammation of the vocal cords and windpipe that causes noisy, high-pitched breathing and a harsh, barking cough, according to MedlinePlus [3]. It often starts like a cold, and symptoms usually get worse at night and last three to five days [3]. Most viral croup is mild and can be treated at home [3].

Watch for signs of breathing difficulty: breathing fast, the ribs pulling in, the chest sinking, or the belly moving a lot with each breath [2][4]. If your child is working hard to breathe, is limp, sleepy or very irritable, or is not feeding or drinking, get medical help [1][4]. If you are worried about your child's breathing, call your doctor right away [3].

q: my 6 year old says his chest hurts when he takes a deep breath
text:
Chest pain when breathing deeply can be a sign of asthma, according to the WHO: asthma symptoms include chest tightness that makes it hard to breathe deeply, and they are often worse at night or during exercise [1]. The WHO says symptoms can also be caused by other conditions, so your child should talk to a healthcare provider [1].

Watch for difficulty breathing — ribs pulling in, the chest sinking, breathing fast, or getting tired when walking or running — and for chest pain when breathing, the SEUP says [2]. Go to the emergency department if your child's general condition worsens, if they are listless, sleepy or very irritable, or if breathing becomes difficult [2]. The SEUP also says chest pain or pain in the side when breathing is a reason to go to the emergency department [5].

q: my baby had a seizure last year and has a fever today
text:
A febrile seizure can happen when a child has a high temperature, and it is not usually serious, according to the NHS [3]. Most febrile seizures do not need treatment [6].

If your child has another seizure now: do not move them or try to hold them in place, do not put anything in their mouth, and do not try to lower their temperature by undressing them or sponging them with cold water [5]. Time the seizure.

Get medical help if your child has a seizure [3]. Call your local emergency number if the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, they have difficulty breathing, the stiffness and twitching are on only one side, they are more sleepy than usual for more than 1 hour after it stops, or they have more than one seizure within 24 hours [2]. Do not drive them yourself if they are still having a seizure or are unconscious [2].

q: my 4 year old had a seizure when he was a baby, does that change anything now
text:
A febrile seizure can happen when a child has a high temperature, and it is not usually serious or likely to cause long-term effects, according to the NHS [2]. Children who have had one have a slightly increased chance of epilepsy later in life, but this is rare [3].

If your child has another seizure, keep them safe while you wait for medical help: check the time it starts and ends, protect their head with your hands or something soft, and remove any dangerous objects nearby [4]. Do not move them or hold them in place, and do not put anything in their mouth [1]. After the seizure ends, put them in the recovery position [4].

Get medical help if your child has a seizure for the first time, one lasting more than 5 minutes, difficulty breathing, twitching on only one side, more sleepiness than usual for over an hour afterwards, or more than one seizure within 24 hours [5].

q: my 7 year old says her neck hurts with a fever
text: A fever with a stiff neck needs urgent medical attention, according to the NHS [7]. While you get help, do not undress your child or sponge them down to cool them, and do not cover them in too many clothes or bedclothes [7]. A high temperature is usually the body's natural response to fighting an infection like a cough or cold, and it normally returns to normal within 1 to 4 days [1]. If your child is able to swallow and is not drowsy, confused or breathing badly, you can give paracetamol or ibuprofen for the fever — the dose depends on their weight, and PediBot's dose calculator can work it out for you [2][7]. Do not give aspirin to a child under 16 [7].

q: my child has a sore throat and white stuff on the tonsils
text:
A sore throat with white patches on the tonsils can be tonsillitis, an infection of the tonsils that is a common childhood illness [1]. The tonsils may be red and swollen, and some children get pus-filled spots or white patches on them [1].

For comfort, have your child drink plenty of water, eat cool or soft foods, and rest [6]. Older children can suck ice cubes, ice lollies or hard sweets, but do not give young children anything small and hard to suck because of the risk of choking [6]. Gargling with warm, salty water can help soothe a sore throat, but children should not try this [6].

See a doctor if the symptoms do not go away within 1 week, or if your child keeps getting throat infections [2]. Get help right away if your child has a sore throat so painful it is difficult to eat or drink [2].
